title: Serious crimes, deaths dotted outgoing year
article: The two biggest criminal cases to hit the territory's courts this year involved a guilty plea that just wouldn't go away and a sexual predator who was put away for a long, long time.
Thomas Sharp, a repeat sex offender, became the territory's first dangerous offender this past fall.
Over three weeks, Yukon Supreme Court heard from two forensic psychologists, innumerable reports and several correctional officers about the man's troubling and often bizarre behaviour.

The previous fall, the 41-year-old Sharp had been found guilty at trial of forcibly seizing a young woman after she stepped off a city bus. He pleaded guilty shortly afterward to kidnapping and sexually assaulting another young woman at knifepoint near the Yukon River.

After weighing the mountain of documentary evidence and live testimony, the territory's chief Supreme Court judge ruled there's no evidence Sharp can be treated for sexual offending in a set period of time. The man was jailed indefinitely under the dangerous offender legislation reserved for virtually unreformable serial criminals.
Sharp has since filed an appeal of both his dangerous offender designation and the forcible seizure conviction.

Also under appeal and slated for hearing in the new year is the 18-month conditional sentence handed down to Wendy Reid, a former office clerk convicted of stealing just under $213,000 from Porter Creek Super A.

The fact she stole thousands from her boss over a 3 1/2-year period using a loophole in the company's bookkeeping system kept coffee shop pundits in gossip, but it was how the conviction was made official that kept her name in the headlines for months.

Back in May, her then-lawyer entered a guilty plea on her behalf - - she wasn't in court that day -- and set the matter over for a sentencing hearing. After her sentencing hearing, which was adjourned, Reid asked to withdraw her guilty plea.
She said she hadn't agreed to the plea, but that her lawyer had entered it anyway.

Judge Heino Lilles rejected the woman's argument the plea was entered involuntarily and let the conviction stand, as did a Supreme Court judge who ruled that despite irregularities in the process, the guilty plea would remain.

Reid appealed her case, but later abandoned it. The Crown, however, hasn't dropped its case for sending the woman to a federal penitentiary. While the prosecution had asked for a three-year jail stint, Lilles opted instead for a conditional term to be served in the community, ruling Reid isn't a danger to the public.
Two other Yukoners were deemed dangerous enough this year by the courts to label them as long-term offenders.

If Chris Schafer, a 26-year-old man originally from Old Crow, hadn't shown remorse for breaking into an apartment and terrorizing two teenage girls at knifepoint -- and trying to rape one -- the Crown would have asked that the man be made a dangerous offender instead, a prosecutor told a court this past fall.
The presiding judge also noted the young man isn't likely to stop committing crimes unless he kicks booze and drug addictions one psychiatrist called "indomitable."

Neither Schafer nor Ross River's Frank Ralph Ladue, 41, fought the long-term offender designations. Both were sent to federal penitentiaries and will then be subject to years of community supervision by a parole officer.
Ladue's conviction for break, enter and sexual assault is the third on his record, leading a judge to call him a "serial" sexual offender.

The territory's first homicide in two years was a story that could be culled from newspaper archives a century ago. A dispute between feuding placer miners on the outskirts of Dawson City ended with one dead and another charged with murder.
Kieran Daunt, 49, faces a preliminary hearing for second-degree murder in January.
Robert Truswell, 53, another Bonanza Creek miner, was found dead from a gunshot wound in late August.
A pinky finger and some shadowy drug debts landed a motley gaggle of Whitehorse residents -- and their various nicknames - firmly in the spotlight since June.

A man who arrived in the Yukon in February for the purpose of selling cocaine and suspected of ripping off local addicts was beaten with a baseball bat before his pinky was severed with a meat cleaver.
Charges were dropped against two people involved, both addicts. Two others, including a 19-year-old, were sent to a federal penitentiary for their parts in the attack.

Their victim, tagged "Mad Dog", received some lasting injuries. The rarely-heard details of day-to-day life in the drug subworld -- casual violence, desperation and cracked lives -- proved the most fascinating, leading to several reporters sitting on courtroom benches for every appearance.
Another form of violence that doesn't often make front pages involved the arrest and conviction of a Liard First Nation chief for domestic assault.

Daniel Morris' June arrest had far-reaching effects. A forum on violence was held in the community, and it took an elders' petition and a lawsuit against the first nation before Morris resigned his post as chief. He's to be sentenced in February.
The year 2003 saw two coroner's inquests into tragic deaths, while a devastating weekend in September will lead to another pair of similar inquests.

Yukon health and police officials travelled to Anchorage, Alaska, to examine a civilian-run facility for intoxicated people to safely sleep off high levels of booze. The trip came at the recommendation of the coroner's jury that heard details of Madeleine Henry's death.

The 41-year-old woman stopped breathing on an RCMP detachment cell floor after she'd been found lying, heavily intoxicated, in a parking lot and arrested. A committee of Whitehorse officials was struck in the fall to examine better ways to care for drunks.

Changes in the way the territorial government's child protection services handle high-risk cases were instituted after two-year-old Emily Sam's death in 2002. A coroner's jury found Sam's death unnatural but undetermined after the September 2003 hearing.
The jury heard the toddler was surrounded by people who drank, and had no sober adults caring for her the night she was found not breathing.
Two more coroner's inquests are in the works after Heather Lynn Benson, 37, and Clark Whitehouse, 34, died separately in RCMP custody on the same highway.

A Carcross RCMP constable was transporting Benson to court in the early morning hours of Sept. 27 when the police cruiser crashed on the South Klondike Highway. Benson was killed instantly. An Outside prosecutor is currently reviewing the case to determine if the policeman should face charges.
The next day, a traffic cop investigating the crash that killed Benson pulled over an unrelated truck driven by Whitehouse, who fled.
As he ran from the officer, the man ingested a quantity of cocaine and died soon after. A fatal amount of the narcotic was found in his system.
No dates have been set for the inquests.

After an epic three-month civil trial last summer, a Yukon Supreme Court decided in March to award Trans North Air an equally record-breaking $14.3 million in damages for a massive 1999 fire that destroyed its airport hangar.
North 60 Petro and two of its employees who removed a company sign from the Trans North hangar roof with a cutting torch, igniting the structure, were found liable.
North 60 is appealing the finding.
Not everything had a sad ending in the crime and punishment world -- just ask two moose in Faro, a drug dog named Luke and some modern- day cowboy Mounties.

Faro RCMP's Cpl. Ken Alderson made national headlines in June when he and several other locals faced a furious cow moose trying to protect its newborn calf, stuck behind a fence in the local conservation officer's backyard.
Because the calf was too little to simply step over the fence, and because mama moose wouldn't let anyone near it, Alderson and company couldn't simply walk up and lift the calf over.

Armed with an RCMP taser he'd never used before, Alderson stunned the cow while two others ran in, grabbed the calf and lifted it over the fence. Everyone -- including the two moose -- promptly hoofed it out of the immediate area.
The taser, intended for use against violent human suspects, was credited with saving the animals' lives as the cow moose had started lunging at the increasing number of bystanders.

And though it happened in Alberta, the RCMP border unit's drug dog, a Labrador retriever named Luke, made Yukon headlines when he stumbled across a cache of marijuana worth millions during a morning jaunt with his handler.

Const. Wayne Smyth and Luke were in Lethbridge training and preparing for their annual recertification when the dog smelled the drugs. The find led Lethbridge police to a huge drug bust and landed several people with drug charges.
Luke and Smith passed their yearly tests too.
An entire shift of Whitehorse RCMP officers were probably wishing in July they still learned how to ride horses at Mountie school.
Some wag decided it would be amusing to let 18 horses and 15 bulls from the annual rodeo out of their corrals and set them onto Whitehorse streets at 3:00 in the morning.

While members of the RCMP's bike patrol zipped to the downtown rodeo grounds to wake up sleeping cowboys, officers in patrol cars began slowly herding the horses in an effort to get them back to their pen.
While police cruiser-driving cops rounded up the horses -- which made it as far as Fourth Avenue from the waterfront -- the now- awake cowboys found the bulls in a herd along the Yukon River.
